title: Pediatric Gastroenteritis with Dehydration
scenario: An 18-month-old male toddler is brought to the emergency department by his mother for 3 days of frequent watery diarrhea and vomiting. She reports he has had fewer wet diapers and has been unusually sleepy.

lines: 18-month-old male brought in for 3 days of watery, non-bloody diarrhea (8-10 stools/day) and intermittent vomiting. Two other children at home have similar symptoms. Mother reports only 1 wet diaper in the last 12 hours. Child is lethargic but consolable, mucous membranes dry, anterior fontanel sunken, capillary refill 3-4 seconds, no tears when crying. Weight today 10.5 kg (well-child weight 11.5 kg two weeks ago).
Provider notified. Peripheral IV access obtained on second attempt. Labs drawn. Oral rehydration attempted but child vomited. Strict intake and output initiated; diaper weights ordered.
IV isotonic fluid bolus started per order. Ondansetron administered. Child remains sleepy but rousable.
Child more alert and interactive, taking oral rehydration solution in small sips without vomiting. Voided moderate amount of clear urine. Mucous membranes moist, capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Isotonic (0.9% sodium chloride) IV bolus 20 mL/kg over 30 minutes
Ondansetron 2 mg IV once for vomiting
Oral rehydration solution in small frequent sips as tolerated
Strict intake and output with diaper weights
Continuous cardiac and pulse oximetry monitoring
Notify provider for urine output under 1 mL/kg/hr

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: Which 4 findings indicate dehydration and require follow-up?
children.rationale: A sunken fontanel, delayed capillary refill, absent tears, and decreased urine output are classic signs of significant fluid volume deficit in a toddler. Normal oxygenation and being consolable are reassuring.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: For each laboratory value, click to specify whether it reflects dehydration, an electrolyte imbalance, or both. Each value may reflect more than one.
children.rationale: Hemoconcentration raises sodium, BUN, and urine specific gravity, reflecting dehydration; hypernatremia and the diarrhea-related hypokalemia are also electrolyte imbalances.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: Complete the sentence. The nurse determines that the priority problem is {1}, and the most urgent goal is to {2}.
children.rationale: Ongoing fluid losses with tachycardia and delayed capillary refill make deficient fluid volume the priority, so restoring circulating volume takes precedence over comfort or fever measures.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this child.

rows.text: Administer an isotonic IV fluid bolus
Offer oral rehydration solution in small sips
Monitor strict intake and output with diaper weights
Offer plain water and fruit juice freely

children.rationale: Isotonic boluses, oral rehydration solution, and intake/output monitoring correct the deficit safely. Antimotility drugs are contraindicated in young children, and plain water or juice worsens electrolyte imbalance.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: After starting the IV fluid bolus and giving ondansetron, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess capillary refill and heart rate
Measure strict intake and output with diaper weights
Recheck serum electrolytes after the bolus
Resume small sips of oral rehydration solution as tolerated
Withhold all oral intake until diarrhea stops
Administer a potassium bolus by IV push

children.rationale: The nurse evaluates perfusion, tracks output, rechecks electrolytes, and restarts oral rehydration as tolerated. Prolonged NPO status is unnecessary, and potassium is never given by IV push.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: Which findings indicate the rehydration treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: Voided a moderate amount of clear urine

children.rationale: A falling heart rate, brisk capillary refill, moist mucous membranes, and improved urine output all show the fluid deficit is resolving. Ongoing high stool output would indicate the losses are not yet controlled.
